stories.topic: The Book That Sat on the Shelf for Eight Years
stories.summary: Seeing Like a State came out in 1998 and Ajay missed it, even though Brad DeLong had written about it on a blog in his RSS feed. Around 2004, after the UPA government came to power, Lant Pritchett moved to Delhi and gave him the book, along with Chester Barnard's The Functions of the Executive, saying it would change the way he thought about the world. It then sat on his shelf until 2012. When he finally read it, every page felt like an attack on what he believed. He cancelled all his meetings and spent a couple of days reading it straight through, arguing back the whole time.
stories.insight: An unread book on your shelf is not a failure. Its physical presence shapes the day you finally pull it out. The books that change you are often the ones you fight with page after page.
stories.quote: Gentle reader, don't beat yourself up too much because there are all these great books sitting on your shelf. It's a part of life. Our books are our companions.

stories.topic: Newton's 'Shoulders of Giants' Was a Put-Down
stories.summary: When Amit brings up 'standing on the shoulders of giants', Ajay explains that the line is Newton's, and that Newton was a truly mean and unpleasant man. He had a lifelong rivalry with Robert Hooke, who was a hunchback and who had implied that Newton's ideas were built on his own work. The famous line was Newton's put-down of Hooke.
stories.insight: Quotes we treat as gracious can come from petty personal feuds. Being a great thinker and being a nice person are separate things.
stories.quote: it's actually because Newton was a truly mean and unpleasant person.

stories.topic: The Long Shadow of Soviet Collectivisation
stories.summary: Stalin could be pragmatic, but on collectivisation he was a 'bloody minded ideologue'. Rich farmers resisted the state taking their land, and he crushed them brutally. In Ukraine he blocked food from coming in and seized the grain, and somewhere between 4% and 10% of the population died in a man-made famine. In 1991, 90% of Ukraine voted to leave. Decades later, by the mid-80s, the Soviet economy survived by exporting crude oil and importing grain. When crude prices fell and grain prices rose, the USSR collapsed.
stories.insight: One top-down scheme played out over sixty years. It planted a nation's lasting hostility and left the empire unable to feed itself, which in the end helped bring it down.
stories.quote: the seeds of the nineteen ninety one referendum where ninety percent of Ukraine voted to leave Russia was sowed in 1932 when Stalin crushed the opposition of Ukrainian farmers against the government grabbing their land

stories.topic: Aadhaar Was Built Before the Privacy Law
stories.summary: Ajay took part in the Aadhaar debates. The first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009, on the understanding that Manmohan Singh's government would bring in a privacy law alongside it. Ajay read Scott only in 2012. Today he says the order was wrong: the privacy law should have come first, strong enough to match the dangers of a single number that can be traced to every person in the country.
stories.insight: Once a state legibility system is built, it is very hard to undo, and the promised safeguards may never arrive. Insist on the checks and balances before the system is built, not after.
stories.quote: Please note the first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009 and James C. Scott was slapping me around in 2012.

stories.summary: Amit recalls an earlier episode about Mao's high modernism. Mao ordered sparrows to be killed because they were eating crops. But sparrows ate locusts. With the sparrows gone, the locusts multiplied, destroyed the crops, and millions starved.
stories.insight: Ecosystems and societies are webs. Pull one thread on the strength of a simple top-down theory and the effects can be catastrophic.
stories.quote: Locusts proliferated after sparrows were killed and actually destroyed all the crops and millions of people starved to death.

stories.summary: Amit admits he was born in Chandigarh, a city designed by Le Corbusier, whom he calls one of the villains of high modernism. On a recent visit with friends, he conceded that the roads are wide, the air is clean and it looks nice. But he knew there was a cost underneath. Ajay added that a great modern living city is not Chandigarh.
stories.insight: The benefits of a planned city are easy to see. Its costs, the organic city life that never got to grow, are the unseen.
stories.quote: Deep down inside I know the unseen, I know the cost.

stories.topic: The Jane Jacobs Chapter Cut from The Power Broker
stories.summary: Robert Caro's The Power Broker was originally more than a million words. The publisher, looking at how thin the paper would have to be, said the book would fall apart beyond a certain length. So a section of about 100,000 words on Jane Jacobs was removed.
stories.insight: The two opposing philosophies, Robert Moses's high modernism and Jane Jacobs's respect for organic order, nearly appeared in the same book. A physical limit of bookbinding shaped the canon.
stories.quote: So they took out a hundred thousand words on Jane Jacobs.

stories.summary: At 18 or 19, Amit and a college friend tried to stage Girish Karnad's Tughlaq as a two-man play. The project fell apart through Amit's procrastination. He explains that Tughlaq was a high modernist who shifted his capital and tampered with the currency, and all of it failed. Karnad wrote the play in the mid-sixties, when disillusionment with Nehruvian socialism was setting in, so the play was also about Nehru.
stories.insight: Art can criticise the present by dressing it up as history. And admiring Nehru does not prevent you from seeing his follies.
stories.quote: This shows that people contain multitudes. Great follies can be made by great men.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: The book the whole episode is about. Amit opens by calling it a remarkable book that profoundly changed Ajay's life.
recommendations.reason: It covers political philosophy, sociology, anthropology, urban policy and development studies, and it gives you a toolkit (state legibility, high modernism, metis) that you can apply almost anywhere. Ajay says even every YouTube creator should read it.

recommendations.creator: The Velvet Underground
recommendations.context: Amit's opening analogy. It was said that only thirty people bought their albums and all thirty became musicians.
recommendations.reason: The band is a model for James C Scott: little known to the public, but hugely influential on the people who go on to influence everyone else.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay raises it while explaining why a less famous thinker like Scott matters.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the theory of change behind the show: the world improves through a long relay of ideas, and you have to see everyone who passed the baton, not just the final runner.

recommendations.item: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots (review of Seeing Like a State)
recommendations.creator: Brad DeLong
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions that DeLong wrote about the book on his blog, which was in Ajay's RSS feed, though he missed it at the time. The show notes link the review.
recommendations.reason: An economist's engagement with the book, and the place where Ajay could have discovered it first.

recommendations.creator: Chester Barnard
recommendations.context: The other book Lant Pritchett gave Ajay in 2004, along with Seeing Like a State.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett offered the two together as books that matter. It appears in the episode as part of how Ajay came to Scott.

recommendations.item: Accidental Politicians (Ep 108 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Ajay names Nehru as a high modernist he nevertheless loves.
recommendations.reason: In that episode Ajay talked about his admiration for Nehru, the background to his point about separating the art from the artist.

recommendations.item: Metrics for Intervention (Ep 101 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites its four metrics while explaining why it is so hard for a state to see.
recommendations.reason: Its four metrics (discretion, number of transactions, stakes, transparency) map directly onto the difficulty a bureaucracy has in seeing the world accurately.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Raised in the discussion of the state endlessly collecting and storing data.
recommendations.reason: It argues that deleting data should be the default, and that the state should have to justify keeping anything.

recommendations.item: A Passion for Cycling (Ep 53 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's suggested starting point for Ajay's challenge to link any EIE episode to Seeing Like a State.
recommendations.reason: Amit jokes that cyclists riding in slipstream formation look like high modernism, while the 'washing machine effect' near a sprint finish resembles spontaneous order.

recommendations.creator: Freedom House
recommendations.context: Ajay's starting point for judging which state legibility mechanisms a country can safely adopt.
recommendations.reason: It ranks democracies from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom. Ajay argues that the right level of state legibility should depend on where a country sits on this list.

recommendations.item: India Needs Decentralization (Ep 47 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited when Ajay argues that decentralisation follows directly from Scott's critique of high modernism.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case for subsidiarity in a country as large and varied as India.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep 37 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of applying Scott's toolkit outside the state.
recommendations.reason: Ajay describes it as 'metis in firms': a giant national bank run through one manual is high modernism, because UP is not Maharashtra.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it for market failure as the reason for state action, and for its chapter title taken from Deng Xiaoping, 'Cross the River by Feeling the Stones'.
recommendations.reason: It shares Scott's message of humility: there is a role for the state, but move in small, reversible steps.

recommendations.creator: Robert A Caro
recommendations.context: Amit's first recommendation, prompted by the discussion of high modernism. He has recommended it on the show before.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece that is at once a biography of Robert Moses, a biography of New York, and a study of how power is used, misused and corrupts. Moses designed the city's bridges and parks from the top down.

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Paired with The Power Broker as the opposite philosophy. Ajay adds that Scott draws heavily on Jacobs in Seeing Like a State.
recommendations.reason: Jacobs represents an organic appreciation of spontaneous order and metis, against Moses's high modernism. Amit says everyone has to read her.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: A book both hosts love, recommended after the Chandigarh discussion.
recommendations.reason: It brings solid economic thinking and many disciplines to urban planning, exposes the follies of high modernism, and respects the local knowledge behind why streets and cities work as they do. Ajay notes that Bertaud is not an economist.

recommendations.creator: Peter Wohlleben
recommendations.context: Prompted by Ajay's account of Prussian scientific forestry and metis.
recommendations.reason: It shows that a natural forest is a communicating system, with roots talking to each other and trees adjusting when one is harmed. It made Amit see that planting forty trees together is not an ecosystem, and it challenges the human belief that we have figured everything out.

recommendations.creator: Girish Karnad
recommendations.context: Prompted by Ajay's reference to shifting the capital to Daulatabad. Amit once tried to stage it in college.
recommendations.reason: A play about a ruler whose grand schemes failed, written in the mid-sixties as a veiled comment on Nehruvian socialism. Amit adds that fiction holds truths about the human condition.

core_ideas.concept: Ideas Move the World Through a Relay
core_ideas.explanation: Change does not need a mass-market hit at every step. Ideas emerge, reshape the culture, and eventually change policy. Thinkers like Scott hand the baton to the people who reach the finish line, so judge progress by the whole relay.
core_ideas.quote: Many short-termist people see that last mile that one runner gets across the race and they say, Yay. But you have to see all the people that handed the baton upstream.

core_ideas.concept: Why 1998 Was the Right Moment for This Book
core_ideas.explanation: After the Berlin Wall fell and the USSR collapsed, many people in democracies felt the ideological battle was over. In the middle of the computer and internet revolution, they turned to technocratic social engineering and lost touch with the defence of freedom associated with Friedman and Hayek. Scott's book was a warning against that turn.
core_ideas.quote: It almost felt like now that the USSR is gone, let's be a little bit more like the USSR.

core_ideas.explanation: The book's puzzle is why some of the smartest people led disastrous grand schemes. P C Mahalanobis was a great statistician and was wrong about society. Nehru, whom Ajay loves, was a great artist whose art (his policy) was bad in many ways. Raw intelligence does not protect you from the high-modernist trap.
core_ideas.quote: And yet when it came to thinking about society, his stuff was phenomenally wrong.

core_ideas.concept: State Legibility: A Bureaucracy Cannot See Like a Human
core_ideas.explanation: For a person, seeing is effortless. For a state, seeing means officials recording facts in files that then trigger policy. Every step suffers from discretion, principal-agent problems, bribes and opacity. People also hide from the state, because history shows states using information for taxation, conscription and worse. Assuming that seeing is free is a technocrat's illusion, because in a lab the instruments don't lie.
core_ideas.quote: See, in a state, Policy is a mapping from a state of nature to a state action.

core_ideas.concept: State Legibility Schemes Have Unintended Consequences
core_ideas.explanation: Frustrated by complexity, states force people to become easier to read: fixed surnames, ID numbers, single land ownership. This flattening destroys arrangements that evolved for good reasons. In one example, a farmer owns the land, someone else has rights to the Kharif crop, and a third person grazes cattle on it when it lies fallow. Ajay calls this a Burkean point. Clarity helps the state collect taxes, but it does not necessarily serve the people.
core_ideas.quote: State legibility schemes have unintended consequences.

core_ideas.concept: Legibility Should Flow From the State to the Citizen
core_ideas.explanation: Amit turns the question around. The state exists to serve us, not to rule us, so the government should be fully transparent and accountable to citizens. Normalising citizens being legible to the state turns the proper order upside down.
core_ideas.quote: We don't need to be legible to them. The state needs to be legible to us.

core_ideas.concept: Data Deletion as a Constitutional Default
core_ideas.explanation: When you pay a toll, the state learns where your car was. Ajay proposes that such data be deleted within seconds by default. If the state wants to keep data, it should have to persuade the people, just as every act of state coercion needs the people's authorisation.
core_ideas.quote: In similar fashion, every act of non-deletion of data should be authorized by the people.

core_ideas.explanation: Modernity is good: secular, individualist, free of superstition and tribe. High modernism is the belief that scientists and engineers know best how society should work and should reshape it through centralised schemes backed by state coercion ('one India, one X'). It fails because planners lack local information, and because people respond to incentives by quietly undermining the scheme. Ajay warns that India is in a second wave of it, driven by tech success and weak political philosophy.
core_ideas.quote: High modernism is the belief that scientists and engineers have a superior claim upon knowledge about society.

core_ideas.explanation: Scott took this Greek word into English. Unlike universal knowledge such as special relativity, most knowledge about society is metis. It is gained by doing, it cannot be written down and handed over, and it changes if you move a hundred kilometres. Respecting it, with humility, is the opposite of imposing a manual from above.
core_ideas.quote: Metis is deep experiential knowledge. It's not knowledge in a book. Okay? You have to be there, you have to do things

core_ideas.concept: Scientific Forestry: Legibility That Kills the Forest
core_ideas.explanation: Scott's central example, which Ajay says applies equally to British forestry in India. The forest is reduced to a single goal, timber volume: plant the best-yielding species in neat rows and run experiments over decades (as at FRI Dehradun) on how far apart to space the trees. The result is countable and legible, but it is a fragile monoculture. It degrades the soil and can be wiped out by a single insect or fungus. It ignores the web of fungi, insects and plants that make a real forest resilient. Ajay calls this ignorance passed off as science.
core_ideas.quote: When people in the world of policy use the word science, you should start getting suspicious.

core_ideas.explanation: Things go badly wrong when four elements combine: (1) a high-modernist philosophy, (2) state power used to make society legible, (3) an authoritarian state, and (4) a civil society too weak to push back. Practical advice: in a country with an authoritarian government and weak civil society, be wary of encouraging high-modernist tendencies or improving state legibility.
core_ideas.quote: When you get these four things together, you get absolutely bad outcomes.

core_ideas.explanation: Grand new capitals, from the move to Daulatabad to Brasília, fail because people don't respond to central plans. Ajay cites Bimal Patel's rule: reserve about 40% of land for streets and parks and let people decide the rest, with no master plan and no micromanaging of private land. Bandra Kurla Complex, built as a financial centre, has towers but no room for coffee shops and pavement life.
core_ideas.quote: A financial center is people. It is conversations over coffee that is a financial centre.

core_ideas.concept: The Green Revolution as High Modernism
core_ideas.explanation: India remembers the Green Revolution as the escape from dependence on PL 480 food aid. Seen through Scott, it was a top-down package of MSP, fertiliser subsidies, free power for pumps and a few rice and wheat cultivars. Over the longer term it has worked badly: pesticides in groundwater, cancer clusters, a groundwater crisis, struggling farmers in Punjab and Haryana (the Netherlands, about Haryana's size, exports $140 billion of food), and a national diet heavy in starch.
core_ideas.quote: We filled up the bellies of the people of India with starch.

core_ideas.concept: Humility, Not Abolition of the State
core_ideas.explanation: Scott is not arguing for the state to wither away. We need a monopoly of violence, law and order, and monetary policy. But the state wants arbitrary power the way firms want profit, so it must be met with checks and balances. Make small, reversible moves. Scott even has a footnote saying this is one reason he opposes the death penalty.
core_ideas.quote: The state has a lust for arbitrary power exact as firms have a lust for profit.

core_ideas.concept: Match State Legibility to a Country's Level of Freedom
core_ideas.explanation: Whether a legibility mechanism is safe depends on a country's checks and balances. Electronic payments are reasonably safe in Norway but a prison in North Korea. Medical records held by the state are fine in the UK but unwise in India. Ajay points out that biometric IDs exist mainly in poorer, relatively authoritarian countries. He proposes a research programme to work out which mechanisms are safe at which Freedom House rank.
core_ideas.quote: So certain systems should not be in certain countries.

core_ideas.explanation: India covers 3.3 million square km and is made up of a thousand Singapore-sized locales, so one ruler instructing all of it invites trouble. Every function should sit at the lowest level of government able to perform it. Bombay's transport needs Bombay expertise, and having built Delhi's metro does not qualify you to dictate to every other city. One currency and one military make sense; most other things should be local and competing. Ajay holds up the EU as a model: goods, people and capital move freely while countries make their own laws.
core_ideas.quote: every function of government should be done at the lowest level of government at which it can possibly be done.

core_ideas.concept: Scott's Toolkit as an Engine for Thinking
core_ideas.explanation: State legibility, high modernism and metis apply well beyond governments. Ajay uses them on firms, for example a giant national bank running the whole country through one manual. He challenges listeners to link any EIE episode to Seeing Like a State.
core_ideas.quote: It's a engine for thinking about the world

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit: 'We all stand on the shoulders of giants. And the other quote... is that I couldn't get anywhere because giants was standing on my shoulder.'
Amit's highest praise for Scott: the biggest compliment he can give Lou Reed is that the Velvet Underground is 'the James C. Scott of music'.

Ajay's EIE T-shirt line: volume one, number one is 'Make trade not war', and number two is 'State legibility schemes have unintended consequences'. Amit replies that you could only buy it in triple XL, 'because how will the words fit?'
Amit: 'When I first heard the phrase high modernism, I thought it basically means that you wear shirt pant and you do drugs.'
Amit on how confusingly similar 'modernity' and 'high modernism' sound: 'It's like popularity and populism... They're almost opposite things.'
Ajay on the misuse of 'scientific' in policy: 'So I get offended when anybody says scientific. I'm like dude don't pull the science card on me.'
Ajay on Nehru: 'I'm very comfortable separating art and artist. So this is a great artist and his art was like pretty bad in some ways.'

Amit carries Ajay's challenge over to the cycling episode: what is a formation of cyclists in slipstream 'if not high modernism'? But near a sprint finish there is a 'washing machine effect, which is much like spontaneous order'.

Amit's one acceptable 'one India, one X': 'One India, one YouTube show is an idea I can get behind', since the show is dubbed into other languages. Ajay then complains that when Susan wanted Malayalam dubbing for her stepmother, YouTube offered Hindi but not Malayalam: 'If you keep going like this, you'll have serious problems.'
On his failed college staging of Tughlaq: 'inevitably one of us was Bengali and hint it wasn't him. And therefore the project went to hell and I procrastinated.'
Amit reminds Ajay he once promised seven recommendations and then gave none. Ajay: 'In the next episode I will give you nine recommendations.'

Amit calls James C Scott 'the Velvet Underground of ideas', after the line that only thirty people bought the band's albums and all thirty became musicians. He adds that the Velvet Revolution was named after the band.
A Unix fortune Ajay quotes as a counterpoint to Newton: 'in computer science we stand on each other's shoulders.'
Ajay on scientific forestry: 'explaining a joke is like dissecting a frog. You can understand it, but it kills the frog.' Imposing legibility killed the forest in the same way.
The Domesday Book, which Ajay invokes as the state's basic legibility logic: 'if you have the land, I'll tax you and I want clarity on who has the land.'
The panopticon, Ajay's extreme case: no civilised person would accept a state that can read their email or phone.
Deng Xiaoping's 'Cross the River by Feeling the Stones', a chapter title in Kelkar and Shah's book, used as shorthand for Scott's advice to make small, reversible moves.
'Some bloke in Delhi who thought why don't we go to Daulatabad and shift the capital': Ajay's nod to Tughlaq, paired with Brasília as a failed planned capital.
P C Mahalanobis and the Mahalanobis distance: a great physicist and statistician whose ideas about society were, in Ajay's words, 'phenomenally wrong'.
Le Corbusier and Chandigarh: Amit was born in a city designed by 'one of the villains of high modernism' and applies his own 'seen and unseen' lens to it.
